Images:
  - [Image #0] The image shows a passage of text discussing the concept of engaging in activities for their own sake versus for a specific outcome. The text is presented in black font on a white background.
    
    Here is the text transcribed from the image:
    
    "This doesn't imply discarding the useful outcomes of activities. In fact, I find that when I engage something for its own sake, I'm far more likely to produce virtuosic work. At a meeting of the rationality community, Anna Salamon once argued that to use truth-seeking as solely a means to fight existential risk (x-risk) would compromise the activity of truth-seeking - for instance, by cutting corners while rushing for an answer. So she proposed an alternative: "Rationality for rationality's sake...for x-risk's sake."
    
    It seems that engaging activities as ends is important for not only the absorption of spiritual nutrients, but also - paradoxically - for their usefulness as means. This can be bewildering for a consequentialist to wrap their head around. It may take mental practice to make this shift if one has ported consequentialist patterns to other parts of one's life, viewing life's activities as instruments, mostly good for other things rather than as containing good in themselves."

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand centers on Tyler Alterman's essay 'Effective Altruism in the Garden of Ends' as the primary boundary object. The arc spans 2021-2025, beginning with Yatharth's book-writing aspirations and EA critique threads, crystallizing in August 2022 with Tyler's published essay, then evolving through community reception, emoji debates, contest recognition, and post-FTX scandal reflections. The discourse is primarily constructive rather than dialectical—focused on refining EA through lived experience rather than attacking it. The core insight: treating life activities purely as means-to-ends (instrumentalization) causes burnout and suffering. The community validates this through personal testimony and explores 'fractal altruism' as an alternative framework where ends exist at every scale.

title: EA burnout, but make it a “garden of ends”
summary:
Tyler Alterman dropped a six-month “critique of EA” that wasn’t a dunk so much as a confession: when you treat everything in life as a means-to-the-end of Doing The Most Good, you start living like a paperclip maximizer—and you can burn out so hard you stop wanting to be alive. The line people kept quoting back at him was basically “find the end in every instant”: stop turning relationships, hobbies, even dishwashing into productivity instruments, because instrumentalizing ends makes you engage them in “lower-quality ways.”

The arc really kicks off in the pre-2022 vibe: Nathan Young publicly invites EA critiques (“reply and I’ll respond”), nosilverv gets a mini-viral reframe (“EA is really ‘Efficient Altruism’; Effective Altruism has never been tried”), and various folks circle the same discomfort: C. Harwick compares suffering-minimization to paperclip-maxing (“any worthy goal pursued to the exclusion of others turns destructive”). Then Aug 31, 2022, Alterman posts “Effective altruism in the garden of ends” and the reception is unusually tender: AskYatharth says the real move is asking “who hurt you?”—not as a gotcha, but as the missing diagnostic behind whole moral worldviews. justavagrant_ chimes in with lived-experience validation: turning travel—and now relationships—into a means wrecks the thing itself (“hey it’s me”). RichDecibels lands the most meme-able punch: it’s “wild that it’s so easy to become the Terminator when you fix your attention on preventing AI Terminators.”

It peaks in the weirdly wholesome co-creation phase: Tyler proposes “fractal altruism” (altruism where ends exist at every scale, not only the global maximum) and Twitter immediately turns it into an emoji design war (coral vs leaf vs flower vs boba), with Tyler rejecting coral because it implies “genetically identical” interchangeable members—exactly the homogenizing vibe he’s fighting. The thread then kind of…doesn’t explode into the debate he wanted; Tyler openly says he’s bummed it didn’t spark more proposals, and people tell him to add a call-to-action or just wait for the ideas to percolate. Institutional EA still half-signs off: the essay wins 2nd place in the EA Critique Contest, and at EAGxBerlin he hears from 20+ people privately, which makes him wonder how much burnout/depression is just silently disappearing from the movement.

After FTX, the tone shifts: Harwick complains the anti-EA dogpile is mostly “ha ha weird nerds,” and Tyler suggests “now might be the time” for a new supplement-to-EA movement—while also saying he’s “probably done with movements.” The reason anyone should care is that this isn’t really about EA; it’s about a broader modern failure mode where optimization logic colonizes your friendships, your art, your spirituality, your rest. The thread is basically a warning label for high-agency people: if your moral ambition makes you instrumentalize your own life, you don’t just get less happy—you get worse at the good you’re trying to do.
